text.p: Spanish and Portuguese 10-year bonds could come in for profit-taking over the coming week, with spreads widening slightly versus Bunds, after the recent rapid gains, analysts said.
They said that most of the good news was already in the price with current spreads of around 60 basis points over the German equivalent.

Nevertheless, they said that should the gap widen to 70 basis points then this would serve as a signal for fresh buying of Iberian bonds, assuming expectations for Spain's and Portugal's inclusion in the first wave of monetary union continued strong.
"The (Iberian) 10-years are at...minimum spreads (to the Bunds). They are vulnerable to any external shock," said analyst Valentin Fernandez of Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
"The prices already include every piece of good news and should stop (rising and) ease a little to consolidate," said Serge Goncalves of Royal Bank of Scotland in London.
"But 70 basis points should be the floor," he added.
"Recent sessions have been very good, with a strong tightening of the spread (with the Bund), the time has come for some profit-taking," echoed Giovanni Polastri of 4Cast in London.
A week ago, the spreads with the Bunds were around 73 basis points, giving a clear signal to analysts that the two Iberian markets were going to move increasingly in step.

After the Amsterdam summit, which calmed market fears over the future of the single currency, the (Spanish) Bonos touched a record low of 61 basis points to the Bund. The Portuguese OT hit a minimum of 50 basis points four weeks ago but since then has marched in line with Spain.
"At the moment, a 50 basis point spread represents a virtual 100 percent certainty that the euro (single currency) is going to begin in 1999 with Portugal and Spain," said Fernandez.
Goncalves said that he would recommend sitting the next month out as there was always the danger of bad news from the audit of state finances ordered by the new French government.

"Despite not expecting the (U.S.) Federal Reserve to raise rates...there could be some nervousness about U.S. data. The market is also looking at Italy, beginning with the CPI (consumer price index) due today and news from France," said Polastri.
Although there was the chance that the Bank of Spain would cut its repo on Monday, the impact of this would be to steepen the yield curve rather than strengthen the 10-year bonds, analysts said.
"The Bank of Spain could cut 25 basis points (to 5.20 percent) but it is not completely certain. If it happens, the curve will steepen," said Fernandez.
Despite the disappointing Portuguese inflation figure for May -- with the year-on-year rising to 2.1 percent from 1.8 percent in April -- the yield curve should steepen in Portugal as well.
"The Bank of Portugal could also cut if Spain does," said Nuno Godinho of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"It may not be immediately...but the market is going to start to discount it and our curve will steepen," he said.
The spread between the Spanish two and 10-year bonds is 141 basis points, while that between the Portuguese equivalents is only 118.
